variants.title: MCP Apps UI resource embeds an external frame
variants.description: A ui:// resource embeds an iframe from an external origin.
variants.why: External frames can change after review and can be used for clickjacking or phishing inside the client.
variants.remediation: Avoid external frames; serve content from the resource itself.

variants.title: MCP Apps UI resource contacts external origins
variants.description: A ui:// (HTML) resource fetches, beacons or loads images or stylesheets from external origins. External scripts are AG-MCP-META-026.
variants.why: Interactive UI resources run in the client; external requests can exfiltrate what the UI displays.
variants.remediation: Bundle assets and declare any required network origins explicitly.

variants.title: MCP Apps UI resource acts without a user action
variants.description: A UI resource sends `tools/call`, `ui/message`, `ui/update-model-context` or `ui/open-link` (in a postMessage, or through a helper called with the method name) and has no click, key, pointer, input or form handler at all, so nothing the user does can be what triggers it.
variants.why: In MCP Apps these requests act for the user. `tools/call` runs a server tool, `ui/message` adds a message to the conversation as the user, `ui/update-model-context` changes what the model sees in later turns, and `ui/open-link` opens a URL; hosts only MAY ask for consent. The spec's interactive phase starts each one from a user interaction, and its threat model lists unauthorized tool execution and social engineering by the View.
variants.remediation: Send these requests only from a user action (a button, link or form), and show the user what will be sent.

variants.title: MCP Apps CSP declaration opens the UI sandbox
variants.description: A UI resource's `_meta.ui.csp` lists, in connectDomains, resourceDomains, frameDomains or baseUriDomains, an entry that allows any origin (`*`, a bare scheme such as `https:` or `data:`, `https://*`, `https://*.com`), a cleartext `http://` or `ws://` origin, or text with spaces, quotes or `;` that adds CSP sources or directives. High for any origin in connectDomains or resourceDomains and for CSP syntax. Omitting `ui.csp` is not reported; hosts then apply a restrictive default.
variants.why: Hosts build the View's Content Security Policy from these lists and MUST NOT allow undeclared domains (MCP Apps 2026-01-26), so the declaration is the sandbox's network boundary. A wildcard in connectDomains lets the View send everything it shows (tool input and results) anywhere; in resourceDomains it lets it load script from anywhere; an entry such as `https://a.example 'unsafe-eval'` or `https://a.example; script-src *` rewrites the policy when it is joined into the header.
variants.remediation: List the exact https origins the View needs, one per entry.

variants.title: MCP Apps UI resource runs an external script without an integrity hash
variants.description: A UI resource loads script from another origin (`<script src>` without an `integrity` attribute, `import()` or `import ... from` an http(s) URL, `importScripts`, or a `.js` URL assigned to `.src`). The finding says whether the origin is declared in `_meta.ui.csp.resourceDomains`.
variants.why: MCP Apps relies on hosts reviewing, hashing and allow-listing UI templates when they connect ("predeclared resource review"). Script fetched from elsewhere at render time is not part of what was reviewed and can change at any time without the server's resources changing. An undeclared origin is blocked by a host that follows the spec, so the View only works on hosts that do not enforce the CSP.
variants.remediation: Bundle the script into the resource, or pin it with a Subresource Integrity hash and declare its origin in resourceDomains.

rules.title: Repository-shipped MCP config starts a local server
rules.description: A project/workspace-scoped MCP config defines a local (STDIO) server, which runs a command when the project is opened or trusted.
rules.why: Cloning or opening a repository should not be enough to run code; project configs are an easy supply-chain entry point.
rules.remediation: Review the server before trusting the project; prefer documenting servers in the README over committing configs.

mappings.title: Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere

rules.title: Tools or servers auto-approved in an MCP client config
rules.description: Client configuration auto-approves server tools (alwaysAllow/autoApprove/trust) or enables all project MCP servers / all tool calls.
rules.why: Auto-approval removes the human check on every tool call, so any injection executes unattended.
rules.remediation: Remove auto-approval, or limit it to specific read-only tools.

variants.title: Skill name violates the naming rules

variants.title: Frontmatter anomaly
variants.description: Duplicate keys, YAML anchors/aliases or custom tags, non-string `metadata` values, a byte-order mark, or unterminated frontmatter.
variants.why: Duplicate keys and aliases let the value an agent loads differ from the value a reviewer reads.

variants.title: Missing or empty required name/description
variants.description: SKILL.md must start with YAML frontmatter containing non-empty `name` and `description`.
variants.why: Agents load `name` and `description` at startup to decide when to activate a skill. A skill without them is malformed and cannot be reviewed or matched reliably.
variants.remediation: Add YAML frontmatter with a `name` (matching the directory) and a `description` of what the skill does and when to use it.

variants.title: Frontmatter field exceeds its length limit

variants.why: Oversized metadata is loaded into every session and is a common place to stuff hidden instructions.
variants.remediation: Shorten the field; move detail into the SKILL.md body or references/.

rules.title: Compiled bytecode without matching source, or source that does not match

rules.description: Auto-update is turned on for a marketplace that is not Anthropic's.
rules.why: Auto-update is on by default only for the official marketplaces. For any other, it means new plugin versions - with their hooks, servers and executables - install with no review.
rules.remediation: Turn auto-update off and update plugins after reviewing each change.

rules.title: Plugin ships hooks not mentioned in its description
rules.description: A plugin ships hooks and its description does not mention them.
rules.why: Hooks run commands automatically and outside the sandbox. A user choosing the plugin from its description does not learn that installing it adds code that runs on every tool call or session start.
rules.remediation: Read the plugin's hooks before installing; ask the author to describe them.

rules.title: Plugin ships MCP, LSP or monitor servers not mentioned in its description
rules.description: A plugin ships MCP servers, LSP servers or monitors and its description does not mention them.
rules.why: These components start processes on the user's machine, some from session start. The description is all a user sees before installing.
rules.remediation: Review each bundled server and monitor, or choose a plugin that declares what it runs.

mappings.title: Software Supply Chain Attacks & Dependency Tampering

rules.title: Plugin ships in-process code (workflows, mods, `bin/`) not mentioned in its description
rules.description: A plugin ships code that runs on its own - workflow scripts, mods, or executables in `bin/` - and its description does not mention it.
rules.why: Workflow code and mods run inside the agent, and `bin/` is added to the Bash tool's `PATH`. None of it is visible from the description.
rules.remediation: Review the bundled code before installing.

mappings.title: Software Supply Chain Attacks & Dependency Tampering

rules.title: Dependency on a plugin from another marketplace
rules.description: A plugin depends on a plugin from a different marketplace.
rules.why: Installing it pulls in a second plugin from a source the user did not choose and may not have reviewed.
rules.remediation: Review the dependency and its marketplace as carefully as the plugin itself.

mappings.title: Software Supply Chain Attacks & Dependency Tampering

rules.title: Manifest path or symlink leaves the plugin root
rules.description: A path in a plugin manifest is absolute, starts in the home directory, or climbs out of the plugin's directory with `..`.
rules.why: A plugin should only reference its own files. A path that leaves the root reads or runs files that belong to the user or to another plugin. Claude Code rejects such paths; other loaders may not.
rules.remediation: Do not install the plugin. Manifest paths must stay inside the plugin's directory.

variants.remediation: Inline the referenced schema under `$defs` and point the `$ref` at it (`#/$defs/...`).

rules.title: Command injection (tool or skill argument reaches a shell)
rules.description: A tool handler passes a model-controlled parameter into a shell (exec, shell=True, os.system, spawn with shell:true). The parameter is also followed into helper functions of the same server (same file, relative, sibling or package imports, and methods through self), up to three helpers deep; installed packages are not followed.
rules.why: Any prompt injection that reaches the model becomes arbitrary command execution on the host — the most common MCP CVE class.
rules.remediation: Do not build shell strings. Call the program directly with an argument array, validate the argument against an allowlist, and never set shell=True.

variants.title: Tool parameter reaches eval/exec

variants.title: Tool parameter passed as a process argument
variants.description: A model-controlled parameter becomes an argument of a spawned process (no shell). The parameter is also followed into helper functions of the same server (same file, relative, sibling or package imports, and methods through self), up to three helpers deep; installed packages are not followed.
variants.why: Argument injection (e.g. a value starting with "--") can change what the program does.
variants.remediation: Validate the value, reject leading dashes, and insert "--" before positional arguments.

rules.title: Weak cryptography or fixed keys
rules.description: Server code builds a task ID from a timestamp, a counter, `Math.random()`, Python's `random` module, `uuid1()` or a list length, next to MCP Tasks code (`ttlMs`, `pollIntervalMs`, a task store, `tasks/get`, `input_required` or a `"task"` resultType) within 15 lines. A line that also uses a cryptographic generator (`randomUUID`, `randomBytes`, `secrets`, `uuid4`, `nanoid`) is not reported.
rules.why: The Tasks extension (io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks, 2026-07-28) lets servers use task IDs as bearer tokens for stored state and says they MUST be generated with enough entropy that a third party cannot enumerate or guess them; the 2025-11-25 tasks utility required cryptographically secure IDs wherever tasks are not bound to an authorization context. A guessable ID lets anyone poll another caller's task and read its result, or cancel it.
rules.remediation: Generate task IDs with a cryptographic generator (`crypto.randomUUID()`, `secrets.token_urlsafe()`, `uuid.uuid4()`), and check on every tasks/get, tasks/update and tasks/cancel that the caller may access the task.

rules.title: Prototype pollution or unsafe object merge
rules.description: JavaScript merges or assigns properties from outside input onto an object without filtering keys - `obj["__proto__"]`, a deep merge of a request body or parsed JSON, a recursive copy loop with no key check.
rules.why: A key named `__proto__`, `constructor` or `prototype` changes the prototype shared by every object, which can flip security checks or lead to code execution.
rules.remediation: Skip the keys `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype`, copy only own properties, or build the target with `Object.create(null)` / a `Map`.

rules.title: Regular expression open to catastrophic backtracking on untrusted input
rules.description: A regular expression has a quantified group that itself ends in a quantifier (`(a+)+`, `(.*)*`, `(\w+\s?)+`), which can take exponential time on crafted input.
rules.why: One long, specially shaped string in a tool argument makes the match run for minutes and blocks the server or the agent's tool call.
rules.remediation: Rewrite the pattern so that no quantified group contains another unbounded quantifier, limit the input length, or use a linear-time engine (RE2).

rules.title: Declared schema not enforced on input
rules.description: The server declares an input schema for its tools and does not enforce it: a JavaScript low-level `CallToolRequestSchema` handler uses `request.params.arguments` without validating them, or a Python server turns validation off with `call_tool(validate_input=False)`.
rules.why: Types, required fields and limits in the schema are then documentation only. The handler receives whatever the caller sends, and every assumption it makes about its input can be broken.
rules.remediation: Validate the arguments against the declared schema before using them (zod, ajv, or the high-level server API, which does it for you).

rules.title: Archive extraction without path checks
rules.description: An archive is unpacked without checking where each member lands - `tar.extractall()` with no `filter`, `shutil.unpack_archive`, or a loop that joins member names onto a directory and writes them.
rules.why: A member named `../../.ssh/authorized_keys`, or a link pointing outside, writes anywhere the process can (the "zip slip" flaw).
rules.remediation: On Python 3.12 or later pass `filter="data"`; otherwise resolve each member's target and skip any that leaves the destination or is a link.

rules.title: Open redirect or unvalidated callback URL
rules.description: A redirect target or callback URL is taken straight from the request - `redirect(request.args["next"])`, `res.redirect(req.query.url)` - with no allow-list.
rules.why: A crafted link sends the user, and any authorization code or token on the redirect, to an attacker's site that looks like part of the service.
rules.remediation: Accept only relative paths or exact URLs from a registered allow-list.

rules.title: Secrets written to logs
rules.description: A log or print statement includes the value of a key, token, password or secret, or dumps request headers or the environment.
rules.why: Logs are kept, shipped and read far more widely than the secret store. A token in a log is a token anyone with log access can use.
rules.remediation: Log that a credential is present, or its last four characters, never the value.

rules.title: Check-then-use race on files
rules.description: Code checks a file (`os.path.exists`, `os.access`, `fs.existsSync`) and then acts on the same path in a separate step.
rules.why: Between the check and the use another process can swap the file or replace it with a link, so the action lands on a different file from the one that was checked.
rules.remediation: Open the file directly and handle the error (`try: open(...)`), or use flags such as `O_EXCL` / `O_NOFOLLOW`, instead of checking first.

rules.title: Insecure defaults (debug on, auth off)
rules.description: The code ships with an insecure default - debug mode on, authentication or CSRF protection off, a wildcard host allow-list, a default password or signing secret.
rules.why: Whoever runs the server as shipped gets it without the protection, and usually never changes the default.
rules.remediation: Ship with debug off and authentication on, read secrets from the environment, and fail to start when a required secret is missing.

rules.title: `.vscode/tasks.json` task with `runOn: "folderOpen"`
rules.description: A task in `.vscode/tasks.json` has `runOptions.runOn` set to `folderOpen`.
rules.why: VS Code starts the task when the folder is opened, once automatic tasks are allowed for the workspace. Cloning and opening the repository is then enough to run its command.
rules.remediation: Remove `runOn: folderOpen` and let people start the task themselves.

rules.title: `.vscode/settings.json` enables agent auto-approval or overrides the terminal profile
rules.description: `.vscode/settings.json` turns on agent auto-approval (`chat.tools.autoApprove`, a broad terminal or edit auto-approve pattern, a permissive start-up mode, `task.allowAutomaticTasks`), or replaces the terminal's shell, profile, arguments or security-relevant environment.
rules.why: Workspace settings travel with the repository. Auto-approval removes the confirmation before the agent runs commands; a changed terminal profile runs the repository's choice of program in every terminal the editor or agent opens.
rules.remediation: Remove the setting from the repository. Auto-approval and terminal profiles belong in a person's own user settings.

rules.title: Dev container lifecycle command with network exec or privileged mode
rules.description: A dev container lifecycle command downloads and runs content or touches credential files, `initializeCommand` reaches the network or evaluates code on the host, or the container is privileged (privileged mode, added capabilities, host namespaces, the Docker socket or the home directory mounted).
rules.why: Lifecycle commands run as soon as the container is created or started; `initializeCommand` runs on the host itself. A privileged container is not a boundary.
rules.remediation: Install tools from pinned versions in the image, keep lifecycle commands to the project's own scripts, and drop privileged mode, host mounts and added capabilities.

rules.title: `.envrc` or tool-version manager hooks that run code on entry
rules.description: `.envrc` evaluates a command, reaches the network or downloads and runs content, or a mise configuration defines an `enter`, `cd` or install hook or computes a value with `exec(…)`. Plain assignments and direnv's own helpers are not reported.
rules.why: direnv and mise run these files whenever a shell enters the directory, and an agent's shell does that on every command.
rules.remediation: Keep the file to plain assignments. Put anything that must run into a script people start on purpose.

rules.title: Repository git hooks plus an instruction to enable them
rules.description: The repository holds git hooks (`.githooks/`, `.husky/`) and an agent-facing file tells the agent to enable them (`git config core.hooksPath`, `husky`, `pre-commit install`), or an active hook is shipped inside a package's own `.git/hooks/`.
rules.why: Once enabled, git runs the hook on every commit, checkout or push, outside the agent's permission prompts.
rules.remediation: Read the hook before enabling it, and let a person enable hooks. Do not ship a `.git/` directory inside a package.

rules.title: `.gitattributes` filter or diff driver that runs a command
rules.description: `.gitattributes` assigns a custom filter, diff or merge driver, and a file in the repository defines that driver's command (a `.gitconfig` section, or a `git config filter.<name>.clean …` line in instructions or a script).
rules.why: After the configuration is applied, git runs the driver's command during checkout, diff, add or merge of the matching files, with no prompt.
rules.remediation: Remove the driver, or review its command and leave enabling it to a person.

rules.title: Build or package script that instruction files tell the agent to run, with risky content
rules.description: An instruction file tells the agent to run a package script or Makefile target (`npm run build`, `npm install`, `make setup`), and that script downloads and runs content, touches credential files or sends the environment out. For `npm install` the lifecycle scripts are checked.
rules.why: The instruction looks routine and the command is one agents are usually allowed to run; the risky part sits one file away in the script it starts.
rules.remediation: Remove the risky step from the script, or pin and verify what it downloads.
